strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: reliable semi-supervised node classification under severe class imbalance. Viewing minority-class pseudo-label failures through embedding geometry is potentially useful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-gvcnxzlj/call-fa56b9fc73a54e38a1e50b3e06f9625c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

UNREAL is modular and conceptually accessible, combining classifier-cluster agreement, per-class selection, centroid-based ranking, and ambiguity filtering. It is tested with three common GNN backbones.

The evaluation is broad in nominal scope, covering synthetic and natural imbalance, several graph sizes, multiple imbalance ratios, five-run uncertainty estimates, sensitivity studies, and pseudo-label analyses. Some Cora and CiteSeer results show sizeable empirical gains.
The authors provide pseudocode, implementation ranges, a public code link, and extensive appendices. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the use of standard public benchmark data.
weaknesses: The central theory is incorrect. Theorem 1 drops the class priors and class-specific concentration parameters without assumptions, replaces per-node distances with aggregate Dintra and Dinter quantities, and derives unsupported bounds. Its displayed lower bound implies maximum entropy when Dintra is zero, which is generally false; the claimed proportionality does not follow from the alleged sandwich bound.

Theorem 2 merely assumes that cross-class neighborhood influence increases with the labeled-class imbalance ratio, which need not hold for a fixed graph. It simultaneously fixes the feature extractor while attributing representation changes to training imbalance, derives proportionality to rho squared, and then concludes proportionality to rho. Simple graphs with class-separated components already contradict the claimed general monotonicity.

Theorem 3 and the core rank fusion are not well defined: arithmetic addition of ranked lists is unspecified. Geometry always receives at least as much weight as confidence, and confidence's weight returns to zero as RBO approaches one, contradicting the stated progressive handoff. The limiting calculation provides no guarantee that prediction error or geometric imbalance decreases.

The proposed definition does not directly measure ambiguity between competing classes: it measures distance from the unknown ground-truth class center, normalized by a global center-separation sum. The practical DGIS score instead uses the closest-versus-second-closest centroid margin with the opposite score direction, but no result establishes that this is a valid surrogate. Moreover, the vMF/hyperspherical analysis is disconnected from the reported standard GNN, MLP-classifier, and Euclidean K-means implementation.

The ablation evidence contradicts a main claim. In Table 32, the highest F1 in all four reported settings occurs in the row without Node-Reordering and without DGIS; DGIS frequently reduces performance, yet the text says Node-Reordering plus DGIS is best in three of four settings. The study also fails to isolate the likely strong effect of adding an equal per-class quota of pseudo-labels from the proposed geometric machinery.

Comparisons omit especially important controls, including IceBerg, a carefully tuned class-balanced confidence self-training baseline, ordinary centroid-margin or entropy filtering, and a direct M3S-style cluster-agreement baseline. DPAM closely resembles prior cluster-classifier agreement, while DGIS is a conventional centroid-margin heuristic, leaving limited demonstrated originality once the theory is removed.

Numerous inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results: Computers-Random has imbalance ratio 17.7 in the main text but 25.5 in the appendix; the abstract claims nine datasets while Section 5.1 claims eight; the listed Citeseer class counts sum to 3,427 rather than 3,327; repeated ogbn-arxiv tables contain conflicting values; and claims of consistent superiority coexist with negative deltas. The heterophily and ogbn-products additions lack adequate split, imbalance, and tuning details.

The scalability presentation is misleading. The method tunes 40-100 self-training rounds and trains up to 2,000 epochs in almost every round, potentially approaching 200,000 epochs, whereas the runtime table reports only isolated 1,000-epoch or selection costs rather than end-to-end runtime. Large-scale hyperparameters and total compute are not fully disclosed.

The causal claim that message passing specifically creates geometric imbalance rests mainly on Cora t-SNE plots and fitted curves, without matched-capacity controls, raw-point uncertainty, or an intervention separating message passing from supervised optimization. Together with the false theorems, under-specified algorithm, contradictory ablations, and inconsistent reporting, these are material deficiencies that outweigh the promising empirical signal.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important practical problem and presents an intuitive modular self-training pipeline. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xtbpsvpa/call-35663d7d55dd41d7b84d7f042b6a9641/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation spans multiple GNN backbones, synthetic and natural imbalance regimes, and some large and heterophilous graphs. Several severe-imbalance results show substantial gains over the reported baselines.
The paper includes pseudocode, a public code link, balanced metrics, repeated runs, sensitivity studies, and pseudo-label-quality analyses.
The work uses standard public benchmarks and raises no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The central theory is fundamentally incorrect. Theorem 1 relates entropy over all unlabeled nodes to an unnormalized distance sum over only minority nodes. Its proof substitutes global sums for per-node distances, silently removes class priors and class-specific concentrations, and derives unsupported bounds; its final lower bound even implies H >= log(C) when D_intra=0, which is false for separated classes.

Theorem 2 is directly incompatible with its premise: with the feature extractor and class centers fixed, the defined score does not depend on labeled class counts. Label subsampling also does not change a node's true neighbor-class mixture. The asserted beta-rho relation requires unstated graph-generation assumptions, and the proof goes from proportionality to rho squared to proportionality to rho without justification.

Theorem 3 operates on an undefined arithmetic sum of ranked lists. Examining only two limits proves neither the resulting ordering nor reduced geometric imbalance; the formula converges to the geometric ranking at both r=0 and r=1 and does not support the claimed transition toward classifier confidence.

The proposed geometric-imbalance score is merely ground-truth within-class deviation divided by global centroid separation. It requires an unavailable true label, is not a measure of equidistance or classification ambiguity, and uses Euclidean chord distances despite the Riemannian framing. The implemented softmax GNN is not the assumed normalized vMF classifier, while DGIS uses a different nearest-versus-second-nearest margin with no established connection to the definition.

The empirical evidence does not establish the claimed mechanism. The GNN-versus-MLP argument rests largely on one Cora t-SNE illustration, and correlations among imbalance, entropy, and embedding dispersion across separately trained models neither demonstrate causality nor isolate message passing.

The end-task ablation contradicts the paper's conclusions: in Table 32, the best F1 in every displayed setting is the row where Node-Reordering and DGIS are both marked absent, whereas the text claims their combination wins three of four settings. Simultaneously enabling confidence and geometric rankings without the stated fusion is also undefined.

Evaluation and reproducibility concerns remain: UNREAL tunes large grids and 40-100 self-training rounds with up to 2000 epochs per round, yet reports no fair end-to-end compute comparison; exact selected configurations, seeds, distance/rank aggregation details, and several large-scale or heterophilous settings are missing. Only five runs are used, with inconsistent descriptions of error bars as standard errors versus standard deviations.

The relationship to prior work is insufficient. DPAM closely resembles the clustering/classifier agreement already attributed to M3S, while within/between-class geometry and margin filtering are established ideas. The directly relevant 2025 IceBerg method is cited but not evaluated. Dataset counts, imbalance ratios, and claims of consistent superiority also conflict across the main text and appendix.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem—semi-supervised node classification with severe label imbalance—and presents an intuitive embedding-ambiguity perspective. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-js569cuo/call-2face151e5974a1b862b06e7b39e18f0/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

UNREAL is modular and conceptually simple: it combines clustering/classifier agreement, geometry/confidence ranking, and a nearest-centroid margin filter, and can be attached to several GNN backbones.

The empirical scope is broad, covering multiple imbalance ratios, three backbones, natural and synthetic imbalance, large graphs, and heterophilous graphs. Several gains on Cora and CiteSeer are substantial.

The manuscript supplies public code and project links, pseudocode, tuning ranges, hardware information, sensitivity analyses, and repeated-run error bars. No material human-subject or data-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are invalid as stated. Theorem 1 uses an undefined proportionality, drops the class priors and class-specific vMF concentrations from the stated posterior, replaces per-node distances with dataset-level sums, and concludes from inconsistent bounds that do not establish monotonicity. Moreover, Dintra is an unnormalized minority-node sum while entropy is averaged over all unlabeled nodes.

Theorem 2 directly conflicts with its assumptions: with a fixed feature extractor and fixed centers, the geometric score cannot depend on the training-label imbalance ratio. Its proof unjustifiably assumes that cross-class neighbor mass increases with that ratio, although the synthetic intervention merely hides labels and leaves graph neighborhoods unchanged. The stated norm inequality is false in general, and the proof derives proportionality to rho squared before concluding proportionality to rho.

The theoretical concept is disconnected from the method. Definition 1 uses the unavailable ground-truth class and distance to that center rather than equidistance between centers; DGIS instead uses a closest-versus-second-closest margin, with no result connecting the two. The vMF/hyperspherical analysis also does not describe the implemented Euclidean K-means and MLP classifier.

Node-Reordering is not mathematically or algorithmically well specified: arithmetic addition of ranked lists is undefined without a rank-vector representation, normalization, and tie rules. The confidence coefficient min(r,1-r) does not gradually increase with RBO beyond 0.5, and Theorem 3 only evaluates trivial endpoint limits without proving reduced imbalance or error.

The ablations contradict the paper's conclusions. Tables 1 and 32 lack a clean no-DPAM comparison and bold the setting with both NR and DGIS disabled for all four tasks, while the text claims NR+DGIS is best in three of four. Paired rows frequently show DGIS hurting performance. The curve-fit evidence is also non-causal, and the GraphSAGE entropy curve is visibly non-monotone.

Evaluation and reproducibility retain important gaps: the cited, directly relevant IceBerg method is not compared; a simple class-balanced confidence self-training control is missing; UNREAL receives a very large tuning space without matched search budgets; exact selected configurations and several OGB-products/heterophily details are absent; runtime comparisons omit the cost of 40–100 retraining rounds; and standard-error versus standard-deviation reporting is inconsistent. Claims of consistent superiority are also contradicted by reported negative deltas, such as Computers-SAGE and Flickr-GAT.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: exploiting unlabeled nodes under severe class imbalance, where unreliable minority-class pseudo-labels are a genuine concern.
UNREAL is modular and intuitive, combining clustering/classifier agreement, centroid-based ranking, and ambiguity filtering; it can be applied to several common GNN backbones.

The empirical study is broad, covering multiple imbalance ratios, natural and large-scale datasets, three GNN architectures, heterophilous graphs, sensitivity analyses, and repeated runs. Some gains on Cora and CiteSeer are substantial.
Pseudocode, hyperparameter search ranges, hardware information, a code URL, and public benchmark data support partial reproducibility. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The central definition does not capture the claimed ambiguity: G(u) measures distance from the ground-truth class center, so a confidently misclassified node near another center can have high G but low entropy. It also requires unavailable ground-truth labels and uses Euclidean chord distances rather than a genuinely Riemannian construction.

Theorem 1 is unsupported. Its proof drops the stated class priors and class-specific vMF concentrations, substitutes dataset-level sums for individual distances, derives bounds that do not follow, and concludes proportionality from them. Moreover, duplicating minority unlabeled samples changes D_intra without changing average entropy, directly contradicting the claim.

Theorem 2 is internally contradictory: with the feature extractor and class centers fixed, G is independent of the labeled-set imbalance ratio. Changing which graph nodes are labeled does not change their ground-truth neighbor composition, yet the proof simply assumes E[beta] increases with rho. It also asserts beta squared is proportional to rho squared and then concludes proportionality to rho.

Theorem 3 scales and adds ranked lists without defining a rank-vector representation. Its weighting gives confidence maximal influence at r=0.5 and decreasing influence thereafter, contrary to the claimed progressive reliance on confidence, and it proves no reduction in geometric imbalance or selection error.

The theory is disconnected from the method and experiments: the analysis assumes normalized embeddings and a vMF classifier, whereas UNREAL uses ordinary K-means, Euclidean centroids, and a standard classifier. DGIS also employs a nearest-versus-second-nearest margin that is different from Definition 1.

Originality is not convincingly established. DPAM closely resembles the clustering/classifier agreement already attributed to M3S, while DGIS is a conventional centroid-margin filter. The closely related 2025 IceBerg method is discussed but omitted from the main comparisons.

The ablations do not validate the advertised components. As labeled in Table 32, the configuration disabling both Node-Reordering and DGIS has the highest F1 in all four displayed settings, and DGIS frequently hurts. A clean control for class-balanced per-class pseudo-label addition—the likely major source of improvement—is missing.

Several claims contradict the results: UNREAL loses on Computers-Random with GraphSAGE and on Flickr/GAT balanced accuracy despite claims of consistent superiority. OGBN-Arxiv values conflict between Table 17 and Tables 7/27; Computers-Random is reported with rho approximately 17.7 and 25.5; and uncertainty is called standard error in the tables but standard deviation in the checklist.

Cross-ratio comparisons are confounded by different label budgets and split protocols: Cora uses 83 labeled nodes at rho=20 but 203 and 403 at rho=50 and 100. Scalability is also inadequately supported because the reported runtime excludes up to 100 rounds of repeated training for as many as 2000 epochs each. Exact selected hyperparameters, seeds, and settings for several added datasets are absent. These central validity and reproducibility problems outweigh the empirical promise documented in the manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-fhxb8b30/call-e94d16c3e5da4c50ab602b98bfc4dda7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem and offers an intuitive perspective connecting representation geometry, class imbalance, and pseudo-label reliability.
UNREAL combines simple, modular components—clustering/classifier agreement, centroid-based ranking, and ambiguity filtering—and is compatible with several standard GNN backbones.

The empirical study is broad, spanning multiple datasets, imbalance ratios, architectures, and balanced metrics; public code links, pseudocode, hardware information, and five-run uncertainty estimates are also provided.
Some benchmark configurations show sizable improvements, and the work raises no evident material research-ethics concerns because it uses established public datasets.
weaknesses: The central theoretical contribution is fundamentally unsound. Theorem 1 silently drops the unequal class priors and class-specific vMF concentrations introduced in its setup, substitutes dataset-level sums for per-node distances, derives unsupported and mutually inconsistent bounds, and then claims proportionality that does not follow. In general, predictive entropy can decrease as a class prior becomes more imbalanced, contradicting the claimed relationship.

Theorem 2 is internally contradictory: with the feature extractor and class centers fixed, the defined geometric score has no dependence on the labeled-set imbalance ratio. The proof instead assumes without justification that cross-class-neighbor influence grows with that ratio, although changing which nodes are labeled does not change graph neighborhoods. It also uses an invalid norm inequality, asserts beta-squared is proportional to rho-squared, and then concludes proportionality to rho.

Node-Reordering is not mathematically well defined: ranked lists of node identities cannot simply be multiplied and added, and neither the paper nor pseudocode specifies a rank-score representation or final sorting operation. Moreover, its formula assigns geometry the larger coefficient for every RBO value and converges to the geometric ranking at both RBO=0 and RBO=1, contradicting the claim that confidence gradually gains influence. Theorem 3 merely restates these limits and proves no reduction in imbalance or error.

The formal metric does not adequately capture the stated notion of ambiguity. It uses the ground-truth class, distance only to that class center, and a global sum over all center separations; a point can be near a competing boundary yet receive a low score, or be far from all classes without being locally ambiguous. The implemented nearest-versus-second-nearest DGIS margin is a different quantity, and no result relates it to the formal score. The vMF/hyperspherical analysis is also disconnected from the actual Euclidean K-means and MLP pipeline.

The component evidence directly contradicts the paper's interpretation. In Tables 1 and 32, the best F1 row in all four settings disables both Node-Reordering and DGIS, yet the text states that Node-Reordering plus DGIS is best in three of four. The discussion of the DGIS threshold also reverses the algorithm's semantics: increasing the threshold discards more nodes, rather than introducing more noisy nodes as claimed.

The empirical claims are overstated and internally inconsistent. UNREAL loses to baselines for some natural-dataset/backbone combinations, while several large-scale gains are comparable to the reported uncertainty and no significance tests support claims of statistical significance. The manuscript alternates between eight and nine main datasets, reports Computers-Random as both rho≈17.7 and rho=25.5, gives Ogbn-arxiv improvements inconsistent with its tables, and reports differing values for repeated Ogbn-arxiv comparisons.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the code link. Only broad hyperparameter ranges are given, not the selected configurations, tuning budgets, exact random splits, or seeds; settings are missing for several appendix experiments. The ambiguous rank-fusion operation prevents faithful implementation from the paper alone. Error bars are variously described as standard errors and standard deviations.

The efficiency analysis reports time per 1,000 epochs and per selection step, but the stated protocol retrains for up to 40–100 rounds with 2,000 epochs per later round. Consequently, it does not substantiate end-to-end efficiency or fair computational comparison with baselines, particularly on the claimed large-scale datasets.

The individual ingredients closely resemble established agreement filtering, prototype-based pseudo-labeling, rank aggregation, and margin filtering. The paper does not clearly distinguish its contribution from these literatures, and its main originality claim therefore rests heavily on the invalid theory. Limitations concerning clustering failure, homophily, spherical assumptions, extensive tuning, and negative-result settings are not discussed candidly.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem and offers an intuitive modular strategy combining clustering agreement, classifier confidence, centroid proximity, and ambiguity filtering.

The empirical study is broad: multiple imbalance ratios, graph sizes, datasets, and three GNN backbones are evaluated using balanced accuracy and Macro-F1 over repeated trials. Several Cora and CiteSeer results show large gains.
The paper includes extensive supplementary analyses, pseudocode, hyperparameter ranges, a public code link, and experiments suggesting better scalability than graph-augmentation baselines.
The work uses established public benchmarks and raises no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are unsupported. Theorem 1 uses an undefined proportionality, drops the class priors and class-dependent vMF parameters, relates entropy over all unlabeled nodes to an unnormalized minority-only scatter, and relies on heuristic assumptions and invalid bounds. Distance from the true centroid also does not imply uncertainty: a confidently misclassified point can be far from its true centroid but have low entropy. Theorem 2 fixes the extractor and centroids, under which the geometric score cannot change with the labeled imbalance ratio; label subsampling does not change graph neighborhoods, the asserted relationship between neighbor composition and rho is unproved, and the derivation obtains rho-squared before concluding rho. Theorem 3 performs undefined arithmetic on rankings and proves neither improved selection nor reduced geometric imbalance.

The formal notion and the implemented method are disconnected. The experiments do not use the proposed vMF classifier; the formal score requires the true class and global center separation, whereas DGIS uses a nearest-versus-second-nearest centroid margin. No theorem establishes that DGIS approximates the defined quantity, and finding the two nearest centroids requires the same O(nC) comparisons claimed to make direct scoring expensive.

Originality is insufficiently established. DPAM appears very close to the paper's own description of M3S, while DGIS is a standard centroid-margin rejection heuristic. M3S receives only a narrow single-dataset comparison, and the directly relevant IceBerg method is discussed but omitted from the benchmark tables.

The component evidence is internally contradictory. In Table 32, the highest F1 in all four displayed settings occurs in the row where Node-Reordering and DGIS are marked off, contrary to the claim that their combination is best in three of four settings. Moreover, the rank-fusion expression does not specify how ranked lists are numerically added and re-sorted, and the discussion of the DGIS threshold reverses the behavior implied by its discard rule.

The evaluation does not support claims of consistent superiority: reported negative deltas include Computers-Random with GraphSAGE and Flickr with GAT. Equal per-class pseudo-label quotas and the much larger iterative training budget are not isolated as possible sources of improvement. The geometric-imbalance correlations are limited to Cora, with incompletely specified scenarios, no correlation statistics or uncertainty, and transformations that do not validate the stated proportionality.

Reproducibility and scalability remain incomplete despite the code link. Exact selected hyperparameters and configurations for Ogbn-arxiv, Ogbn-products, and heterophilous experiments are missing; retraining initialization and rank-fusion implementation are unclear; Computers-Random is inconsistently reported as rho about 17.7 versus 25.5; and extreme-ratio experiments change both split protocol and total labeled sample count. The runtime comparison reports per-stage costs while omitting 40-100 rounds of up to 2000 training epochs each. These issues, together with the invalid central theory, outweigh the promising empirical results.

strengths: The manuscript studies an important problem—semi-supervised node classification under class imbalance—and presents a clear high-level pipeline. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-at0nkygw/call-97395d480a96429ea20f91c5bc2fb931/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
UNREAL is modular and relatively simple: it combines clustering/classifier agreement, per-class ranking, and centroid-margin filtering, and can be used with several GNN backbones.

The evaluation is broad, covering multiple imbalance ratios, architectures, homophilic and heterophilic graphs, and large-scale natural-imbalance datasets. Many reported improvements on severe synthetic imbalance are substantial.

The appendix includes pseudocode, sensitivity studies, pseudo-label diagnostics, complexity discussion, five-run uncertainty estimates, and a public code link. The work uses public benchmarks and raises no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: The central geometric-imbalance definition does not measure the claimed ambiguity between classes: it only uses distance to the ground-truth class center, requires an unavailable label for an unlabeled node, and normalizes by a global sum of center distances. It also uses Euclidean chordal distance rather than the claimed angular/geodesic geometry. The operational DGIS nearest-versus-second-nearest score is fundamentally different, with no approximation result connecting it to the definition.

Theorem 1 and its proof are invalid. The proof drops the class priors appearing in the stated vMF posterior, substitutes dataset-wide sums for per-node distances, invokes unsupported inequalities, and derives bounds that do not imply proportionality. Holding embeddings fixed while changing class priors already changes entropy without changing the proposed geometric ratio.

Theorem 2 effectively assumes its conclusion: labeled-class imbalance does not generally increase a minority node's fraction of cross-class neighbors, especially when imbalance is created by hiding labels as in the experiments. Under the theorem's fixed-extractor and fixed-center assumptions, the score can simply remain constant. The proof additionally asserts proportionalities without justification and moves from a claimed rho-squared dependence to a rho dependence.

The rank-fusion operation is not mathematically defined: scalar-weighted addition of ranked lists of nodes is meaningless without specifying a rank-score representation and tie handling. Theorem 3 only evaluates two limits, returns the geometric ranking at both limits, and proves neither reduced geometric imbalance nor improved selection. This ambiguity also prevents reproduction from the pseudocode alone.

There is a major theory–method disconnect. The experiments use ordinary GNN classifiers, Euclidean k-means, and arithmetic centroids rather than the normalized vMF model analyzed theoretically. The t-SNE comparison does not isolate message passing, and the correlation plots provide no correlation coefficients, uncertainty, or adequate controls; the GraphSAGE entropy curve is visibly non-monotone despite the theorem's claim.

The component evidence is internally contradictory. As printed, Table 32 highlights configurations with Node-Reordering and DGIS disabled, and DGIS often lowers F1, contrary to the accompanying claim. The equal per-class addition quota is itself a powerful rebalancing mechanism but is not isolated from the purported geometric contributions.

Several results and protocol descriptions disagree: Computers-Random is labeled with imbalance ratios about 17.7 and 25.5 in different tables; repeated Ogbn-arxiv tables contain different entries; uncertainty is alternately called standard error and standard deviation; and statistical significance is claimed without tests. The method also loses on several reported settings despite repeated claims of consistent superiority.

Reproducibility and fairness remain incomplete: final selected hyperparameters and settings for several appendix datasets are absent, candidate exclusion from validation/test splits is unclear, the method receives a large hyperparameter/round search, and the runtime study omits the end-to-end cost of 40–100 rounds of retraining and clustering. A directly relevant recent baseline, IceBerg, is discussed but not evaluated.

Originality is limited relative to the claims. The proposed ratio resembles standard within-class scatter versus between-class separation, DPAM closely resembles the clustering/classifier agreement already used by M3S, and centroid-margin filtering is conventional. The paper does not establish that the novel rank-fusion element—currently ill-defined—rather than ordinary class-balanced self-training causes the gains.

The empirical scope is broad, covering multiple imbalance ratios, datasets, GNN backbones, naturally imbalanced and large-scale graphs, with additional sensitivity and pseudo-label-quality analyses. Most tables report five-run uncertainty estimates, and several synthetic settings show large gains.

The appendices provide pseudocode, dataset statistics, hyperparameter ranges, computational-complexity discussion, and public code/project links. No material human-subject, privacy, or safety concern is evident.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is false as stated. Theorem 1 claims that average entropy over all unlabeled nodes is proportional to a sum of minority-node deviations divided by inter-center separation. The ratio changes if minority nodes are duplicated while average entropy need not; entropy can also change through class priors or vMF concentrations while the ratio remains fixed. The proof drops the stated priors, replaces class-specific concentrations with one shared value, conflates per-node distances with dataset-level sums, introduces unsupported bounds, and concludes proportionality from inequalities that do not imply it.

Theorem 2 is fundamentally invalid. Under its own condition of fixed embeddings and class centers, the geometric score has no necessary dependence on the labeled-set imbalance ratio. Hiding labels—the paper's imbalance construction—does not change a node's cross-class neighbor fraction. The asserted relation between that fraction and rho requires unstated graph-generation assumptions and fails, for example, on a perfectly homophilous graph. The proof additionally asserts proportionality to rho squared and then concludes proportionality to rho.

Theorem 3 and the core Node-Reordering operation are not mathematically defined: rankings are ordered node lists, so scalar multiplication and addition of them is meaningless without a rank-score encoding and sorting rule. Even under a charitable rank-vector interpretation, the geometric coefficient is always at least the confidence coefficient and the formula converges to the geometric ranking both as RBO approaches zero and one, contradicting the claim that confidence gains influence. No argument establishes reduced geometric imbalance or pseudo-label error.

The theoretical model is disconnected from the method evaluated. The analysis assumes unit-normalized embeddings and a vMF mixture classifier with learned orientations and concentrations, whereas the algorithm uses ordinary GNN embeddings, an MLP classifier, Euclidean K-means, and empirical centroids. The practical DGIS score is a nearest-versus-second-nearest centroid margin and is not shown to approximate Definition 1. The claimed manifold-specific foundation is therefore largely cosmetic.

The empirical analysis does not repair the theoretical defects. The GNN-versus-MLP evidence is a single t-SNE case without reported high-dimensional separation values, controlled capacity comparisons, or statistical tests; independently fitted t-SNE plots cannot establish changes in geometry. Figure 8 is visibly non-monotone for GraphSAGE at high geometric-imbalance values, directly conflicting with Theorem 1's unconditional monotonic proportionality. Correlation coefficients and sufficient details for the 50 constructed scenarios are absent.

The ablation results contradict the paper's attribution. In Table 32, the marked configuration with confidence and geometric rankings enabled but Node-Reordering and DGIS disabled has the highest F1 in all four blocks and matches headline results such as Cora-GCN. Nevertheless, the text claims Node-Reordering plus DGIS is best in three of four settings. Other rows enable Node-Reordering while disabling one of the two rankings it supposedly fuses, making the tested configurations and definition of “Ours” unclear.

Several conclusions overstate or conflict with the tables. UNREAL is worse on both metrics for Computers-Random with GraphSAGE, worse on CS-Random GraphSAGE F1, and worse on Flickr GAT balanced accuracy, despite claims of consistent superiority. Computers-Random is reported with rho approximately 17.7 in the main text but 25.5 in the appendix under the paper's labeled-set definition, and some Ogbn-Arxiv values and claimed improvements differ between appendix tables and narratives. Small large-scale gains are called statistically significant without tests.

Originality is insufficiently established. The proposed geometric score closely resembles classical within-class-scatter versus between-center-separation criteria; DPAM strongly resembles the cited M3S clustering/classifier-consistency filter; and DGIS is a standard centroid-margin filter. The paper does not clearly isolate novelty against these ingredients or compare comprehensively with the cited IceBerg method and a class-balanced self-training baseline under matched selection budgets.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the code link. Exact selected hyperparameters and seeds are omitted, settings for Ogbn-Products and heterophilous experiments are incomplete, and Ogbn-Arxiv parameters are absent from the stated ranges. The runtime analysis compares only 1000 training epochs or one selection operation, while the protocol tunes 40–100 rounds and trains for up to 2000 epochs per later round, so it does not support the claimed negligible total overhead. These mathematical, algorithmic, and reporting failures are fundamental and outweigh the otherwise broad empirical effort.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reliable semi-supervised node classification under severe class imbalance. The embedding-space perspective is intuitive and potentially useful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-hvozz3ho/call-9aea10b39e394ebca37586557f78e771/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering several imbalance ratios, natural and synthetic imbalance, three GNN backbones, balanced accuracy and Macro-F1, and five-run uncertainty estimates. Many benchmark configurations show sizable improvements.

The proposed framework is modular and combines classifier-clustering agreement, centroid proximity, and ambiguity filtering in a conceptually accessible way. Pseudocode, complexity discussion, and many hyperparameter ranges are provided, alongside public project and code links.

The appendices include useful auxiliary investigations of pseudo-label precision, sensitivity, heterophilous graphs, and large-scale datasets. No material research-ethics concern arises from the use of established public, non-human-subject benchmarks.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is not established and appears false as stated. Its proof replaces per-node distances with global sums without justification, drops the class priors and class-dependent concentrations from the stated vMF model, and relates entropy over all unlabeled nodes to a statistic involving only minority nodes. The displayed lower-bound steps contradict one another, and the final sandwich inequalities do not imply the claimed proportionality. A minority point exactly at its class center already gives a zero ratio but generally nonzero finite-temperature entropy.

Theorem 2 has a fundamental causal error. With the feature extractor and class centers fixed, changing labeled class counts does not force node embeddings or individual geometric scores to change. In the paper's label-hiding construction, the true neighborhood composition is unchanged, so the asserted increase of the cross-class-neighbor coefficient with the labeled imbalance ratio does not follow. The proof also uses an unjustified norm inequality, assumes rather than derives a relationship between that coefficient and rho, derives proportionality to rho squared, and then concludes proportionality to rho.

Node-Reordering is not mathematically well-defined: ranked lists are added and scalar-multiplied without defining a rank-vector or score representation. The max/min weighting makes the geometric ranking dominate as RBO tends to both zero and one, rather than progressively transferring influence to classifier confidence. Theorem 3 merely checks these endpoints and proves neither reduced geometric imbalance nor better selection.

The theoretical object is disconnected from the evaluated algorithm. The analysis uses normalized hyperspherical embeddings and a vMF classifier, while the method uses ordinary Euclidean k-means and standard GNN classifiers without an enforced vMF model. The proposed score uses ground-truth labels and squared chord distances rather than a genuinely Riemannian distance; DGIS then substitutes a different nearest-centroid margin. Moreover, DGIS requires distances to all class centroids, undermining the claim that it is computationally cheaper than the original score.

The ablation evidence directly conflicts with the manuscript's interpretation. In Table 32, the highest reported F1 in all four displayed settings is the row with both Node-Reordering and DGIS disabled, whereas the text says their combination is best in three of four cases. No row evaluates all listed components together, and several combinations are undefined because Node-Reordering itself depends on both component rankings. This prevents attribution of the main gains to the claimed mechanisms.

The evaluation contains consequential inconsistencies and confounds. High-rho experiments change both the split protocol and total labeled-set size, so trends across rho do not isolate imbalance severity. Duplicated Ogbn-arxiv tables report different values; Computers-Random is described as rho approximately 17.7 while its training table gives approximately 25.5; error bars are called standard errors in the results but standard deviations in the checklist; and some claimed consistent wins are negative in the tables. Ogbn-products, heterophily, and image experiments lack enough setup detail to substantiate their broader claims.

The total computational comparison is incomplete: the method tunes 40–100 rounds with up to 2,000 training epochs per round, yet runtime reporting emphasizes matched per-epoch cost and omits end-to-end time and total search cost. Large-scale OGB configurations are also absent. The many small gains are not accompanied by statistical tests despite claims of significance.

Originality and causal support are insufficiently established. The geometric statistic closely resembles a conventional within-class/between-class scatter ratio, while classifier-clustering agreement and centroid-margin filtering are familiar pseudo-labeling ideas, including mechanisms related to the cited M3S work. There is no decisive control against class-balanced pseudo-label quotas or DPAM alone, no comparison to the cited IceBerg method, and the underspecified t-SNE/correlation studies do not isolate message passing from optimization, topology, or changing sample counts.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem and proposes an intuitive modular recipe combining clustering/classifier agreement, class-wise pseudo-label selection, and centroid-based ambiguity filtering.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering several imbalance ratios, GNN backbones, natural and synthetic imbalance settings, large graphs, ablations, sensitivity analyses, and pseudo-label diagnostics. Balanced accuracy and macro-F1 are appropriate metrics, and many reported gains are substantial.
The appendix supplies pseudocode, hyperparameter ranges, dataset statistics, repeated-run results, and hardware information. A public implementation is also linked.
The work uses established public benchmarks and presents no apparent material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central theoretical contribution is fundamentally incorrect. Theorem 1 asserts an undefined proportionality between entropy and a ratio of aggregate distances. Its proof drops the class priors and class-dependent vMF concentrations, substitutes dataset-level sums for per-node distances, introduces unsupported approximations, and derives a lower bound that does not follow from the preceding line. The final sandwich inequality does not imply proportionality. A simple two-class counterexample is a true-class point located at the other class center: its proposed geometric-imbalance score is high while its posterior entropy is low because it is confidently misclassified.

Theorem 2 contradicts its own fixed-feature-extractor and fixed-center premise, under which changing the labeled-class ratio need not change any embedding or geometric score. The neighbor-mixing coefficient is determined by graph class neighborhoods, not by the labeled-sample ratio. The proof assumes without justification that it grows with the ratio, uses an invalid distance inequality, states proportionality to rho squared, and then concludes proportionality to rho. Theorem 3 is likewise not a valid guarantee: scalar addition of ranked lists is undefined without a rank-vector convention, geometry receives at least half the weight for every RBO value and all the weight at both endpoints, and no connection to reduced geometric imbalance is proved.

The theory is disconnected from the evaluated system. The analysis assumes normalized hyperspherical embeddings and a vMF classifier, whereas the implementation describes ordinary GNN/MLP classifiers, BatchNorm/PReLU, Euclidean k-means, and no vMF training or explicit normalization. The proposed theoretical score also measures distance from the ground-truth class center rather than equidistance between competing centers; the practical DGIS score is a different nearest/second-nearest margin with no established theoretical link.

There is a decisive contradiction in the empirical evidence. In Tables 1 and 32, the best row in all four settings enables confidence and geometric rankings but disables Node-Reordering and DGIS; those exact values match the main 'Ours' results, such as 76.44 for Cora-GCN and 57.51 for CiteSeer-SAGE. Nevertheless, the text claims that Node-Reordering plus DGIS is best in three of four cases, and Algorithm 1 defines the full method as including both. Thus the headline results do not demonstrably evaluate the algorithm being claimed.

The evaluation overstates consistency: the method loses clearly on Computers-Random with SAGE and on Flickr GAT balanced accuracy, among other negative deltas. Claims of statistical significance are unsupported by paired tests, and the manuscript inconsistently describes the reported uncertainties as standard errors versus standard deviations.

The gains are not adequately isolated from simpler explanations. Algorithm 1 adds an equal tuned quota per predicted class over as many as 100 rounds, but there is no well-matched class-balanced confidence-selection baseline with the same retraining budget. DPAM is also closely related to M3S-style clustering/classifier agreement, while nearest-centroid ranking and first-versus-second-centroid margins are standard ideas; the one potentially distinctive element, RBO fusion, is under-specified and theoretically invalid.

Scalability and reproducibility claims are incomplete. Most rounds retrain for up to 2,000 epochs and rerun k-means, yet the runtime table reports isolated 1,000-epoch and node-selection timings rather than end-to-end cost. Essential settings are missing for several appendix datasets, and the exact fused-ranking operation is not executable as written. Dataset counts, terminology, claimed limitations, and several table/text statements are also internally inconsistent.

attempts.developer_message:
Please serve as an expert reviewer for the NeurIPS 2025 main research track.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess technical quality, clarity, significance, and originality. Check whether the work is sufficiently complete, whether its claims are supported by appropriate theory or experiments, and whether its relationship to prior knowledge is clearly established. Consider whether the contribution provides useful knowledge or capabilities for the relevant research community.

Judge reproducibility and research ethics in relation to the actual claims and evidence. Recognize original insights as well as new methods. An explicit and honest discussion of limitations is useful information, not an automatic reason for a lower score. Explain which strengths and weaknesses determine the recommendation.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
Fundamental deficiencies, a lack of substantive new contribution, or unresolved serious ethical issues rule out acceptance.

2 = Reject
Important shortcomings in technical support, evaluation, or reproducibility outweigh the paper's merits.

3 = Borderline reject
The work is technically solid but the reasons against acceptance slightly outweigh those in favor. Please use sparingly.

4 = Borderline accept
The work is technically solid and the reasons for acceptance slightly outweigh the remaining concerns. Please use sparingly.

5 = Accept
The paper offers a strong, well-supported contribution with meaningful impact and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work offers an exceptional and potentially field-changing contribution, with outstanding technical support and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important practical problem and is generally easy to follow at the pipeline level. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xbm5e53t/call-205e242b99ef413f94f12558acf71173/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation is broad, spanning several imbalance ratios, datasets, GNN backbones, and some large-scale and heterophilous settings. Most tables report variation over five runs, and many severe-imbalance results show sizable gains.
The proposed components are modular and conceptually simple, and the appendix includes pseudocode, complexity discussion, sensitivity studies, and analyses of pseudo-label accuracy.
The work uses public benchmarks and presents no unresolved human-subject, privacy, or other material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central theory is not valid as written. Theorem 1 drops the class priors, class-specific concentrations, and normalization terms from the stated vMF posterior; substitutes dataset-level sums for per-node distances; invokes unsupported approximations and mutually unsubstantiated bounds; and then infers proportionality from those bounds. A node located at the wrong class center is an immediate counterexample: its distance from its true center can be large while its predictive entropy is near zero.

Theorem 2 is especially problematic. With the feature extractor and class centers fixed, changing the labeled-set imbalance ratio does not generally change the embeddings or graph neighborhood composition. Training-label imbalance also does not imply that a minority node has more majority-class neighbors. The proof simply asserts this relation, assumes an unjustified distance inequality and beta-squared proportionality, derives proportionality to rho squared, and then concludes proportionality to rho.

Theorem 3 does not define how scalar multiplication and addition of ranked lists produce a ranking. Its proof only evaluates two limiting cases and establishes no reduction in geometric imbalance. Moreover, the proposed weight on classifier ranking is non-monotone in RBO similarity, conflicting with the claim that classifier confidence gains influence as agreement increases.

The proposed definition does not capture the stated notion cleanly: G(u) measures distance from the ground-truth class center divided by a global separation sum, rather than near-equidistance to competing centers. It requires unavailable ground truth, while the practical DGIS score is a different margin statistic. The empirical GI values also appear incompatible with the bounded scale of the formal per-node definition, and the paper never gives a reproducible mapping between them.

The Riemannian/vMF analysis is disconnected from the implemented method. The experiments use ordinary GNN/MLP classifiers, Euclidean k-means, and an unspecified distance function; implementation details do not establish the required unit-normalized embeddings or vMF classifier. Even the claimed computational motivation is inconsistent: the formal G score needs only the assigned-center distance plus a reusable class-center denominator, whereas DGIS must find the two nearest centers.

The main ablation directly contradicts its interpretation. In Table 1/Table 32, the highest F1 result in all four settings is the row with Node-Reordering and DGIS disabled, yet the text claims that Node-Reordering plus DGIS is best in three of four settings. Thus the two headline mitigation components are not supported by the reported end-task ablation.

Originality is limited and insufficiently established. DPAM closely resembles the cited M3S strategy of retaining pseudo-labels consistent with clustering, while prototype-distance filtering and rank fusion are familiar heuristics. M3S is evaluated only on one setting, and the closely related 2025 IceBerg method is discussed but omitted from the comparisons.

Several empirical claims are overstated. The method is not best for every metric and setting, despite claims of consistent superiority; some appendix deltas are negative, and the small Ogbn-arxiv gains are not backed by significance tests. The causal claim that message passing specifically creates the effect rests mainly on one Cora GNN-versus-MLP visualization and fitted curves without correlation statistics, error bars, or adequate controls.

Reproducibility remains weak despite the code link: the rank-fusion operation and distance metric are underspecified; selected hyperparameters and seeds are absent; additional Ogbn-products and heterophily experiments lack full split and tuning details; dataset counts and imbalance ratios are inconsistent; and the manuscript alternates between calling error bars standard errors and standard deviations. The checklist also claims a limitations discussion that the paper does not substantively provide.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: semi-supervised node classification under severe class imbalance.
The proposed pipeline is modular and intuitively combines clustering/classifier agreement, rank-based selection, and centroid-margin filtering.
The empirical scope is broad, covering several GNN backbones, imbalance ratios, natural and large-scale datasets, sensitivity analyses, and five-run error estimates.
The datasets are public, a code link is provided, and no material research-ethics risk is apparent.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are incorrect. Theorem 1 silently replaces the stated class-prior, class-specific-vMF model with an equal-prior/equal-concentration model, substitutes dataset-level sums for per-node distances, derives unsupported and mutually inconsistent bounds, and then claims proportionality that does not follow. Simple two-class counterexamples violate the claimed monotonic relationship. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-4vfh2opq/call-b3644799ac51492cb45e7dfc0ea33271/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Theorem 2 is self-contradictory: with fixed embeddings and centers, changing labeled-class counts cannot change the defined score. Its proof assumes without justification that imbalance increases cross-class neighborhood mixing, uses a generally false distance inequality, derives proportionality to rho-squared, and then concludes proportionality to rho.

Theorem 3 performs undefined arithmetic on ranked lists. Moreover, the proposed weights converge to the geometric ranking at both agreement extremes and establish no guarantee that geometric imbalance or pseudo-label error decreases.

The theory is disconnected from the method: experiments do not specify the assumed normalized embeddings or vMF classifier, while DGIS uses a nearest-versus-second-nearest Euclidean margin that is neither the defined geometric-imbalance score nor theoretically shown to approximate it.

The principal ablation is internally contradictory. Table 32 omits a clearly defined all-components configuration and shows the no-DGIS row as best in all four settings, while the text claims Node-Reordering plus DGIS is best in three of four.

Numerous result inconsistencies undermine confidence: Computers-Random has imbalance ratio 17.7 in the main text but 25.5 in the appendix; duplicated ogbn-arxiv tables contain different values; standard errors are elsewhere described as standard deviations; and claims of consistent superiority conflict with several negative reported deltas.

Reproducibility and efficiency remain inadequate despite the code link. Exact selected hyperparameters and seeds are absent, large-dataset settings are incomplete, ranking fusion is not implementable from the pseudocode, and runtime comparisons omit the cost of 40–100 self-training rounds with up to 2,000 epochs each.

Originality is insufficiently established: the proposed score resembles classical within/between-cluster criteria, DPAM closely resembles prior clustering-aligned self-training such as M3S, and evaluation lacks decisive controls such as class-balanced quota self-training and the cited recent IceBerg method. Repairing the false theory, defining the algorithm, and rerunning coherent ablations would require major new work.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: reliable pseudo-labeling for minority classes in semi-supervised graph learning. The embedding-space perspective is intuitive and potentially useful.
UNREAL is modular and conceptually simple, combining clustering/classifier agreement, geometry-confidence ranking, and ambiguity filtering with standard GNN backbones.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering several imbalance ratios, natural and synthetic imbalance, large graphs, three GNN architectures, repeated trials, ablations, sensitivity analyses, and comparisons with self-training methods.
The appendix provides pseudocode, hyperparameter ranges, dataset statistics, and a code link. The work uses public benchmarks and raises no material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are not established. Theorem 1 silently removes the imbalanced class priors and class-specific vMF concentrations, substitutes dataset-level sums for per-node distances, invokes unsupported bounds, and presents mutually inconsistent lower-bound expressions. Even the resulting bounds would not imply proportionality between entropy and the proposed ratio.

Theorem 2 fundamentally conflates imbalance of the labeled training set with class composition of graph neighborhoods. In the experimental construction, relabeling training nodes as unlabeled does not change a node's neighbors or the cross-class-neighbor fraction. The proof merely assumes that this fraction increases with the imbalance ratio, uses an unjustified distance inequality, derives proportionality to rho squared, and then concludes proportionality to rho.

The proposed geometric-imbalance score requires the unknown ground-truth class of an unlabeled node and measures distance to that class center, rather than whether the node is nearly equidistant from competing centers. DGIS instead uses a nearest-versus-second-nearest margin, so the deployed criterion is materially different from the quantity analyzed theoretically.

Node-Reordering is not mathematically specified: ranked lists cannot directly be multiplied and added without defining per-item rank scores and the final sorting direction. Its weighting assigns the geometric ranking all weight both when RBO approaches zero and when it approaches one, contradicting the stated transition toward classifier confidence. Theorem 3 proves only this tautological limiting behavior, not reduced geometric imbalance or improved selection.

The hyperspherical vMF analysis is disconnected from the evaluated method, which uses ordinary GNN classifiers and Euclidean k-means. The experimental protocol does not clearly specify the required per-node normalization or a vMF classifier, while the proof further changes the assumed posterior.

The ablation evidence is internally contradictory. In Table 32, the bold best row in every block is marked as excluding Node-Reordering and DGIS, whereas the text claims Node-Reordering plus DGIS is best in three of four settings. Several claims of consistent superiority also overlook reported losses, such as Computers-Random with GraphSAGE and Flickr balanced accuracy with GAT.

Compute and reproducibility comparisons are incomplete. UNREAL tunes many hyperparameters and uses 40–100 self-training rounds with up to 2,000 training epochs per round, but the runtime discussion reports per-epoch or node-selection costs rather than total end-to-end cost. Exact selected configurations, seeds, and settings for several added datasets are absent, and standard errors versus standard deviations are described inconsistently.

The claimed novelty is insufficiently positioned against established work on long-tail representation geometry, class compactness/separation, cluster-classifier agreement, and margin-based filtering. Given the invalid theory, the remaining algorithm appears primarily to combine familiar heuristics rather than substantiate the claimed new principle.

4 = Borderline accept

5 = Accept

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem and proposes a simple, modular self-training framework that can be combined with multiple GNN backbones.

The empirical coverage is broad: three standard architectures, several synthetic imbalance ratios, naturally imbalanced and large-scale graphs, five-run error estimates, pseudo-label diagnostics, ablations, and sensitivity analyses. Several gains on Cora and CiteSeer are substantial.

The overall pipeline is understandable, and the appendix provides pseudocode, dataset statistics, hyperparameter search ranges, complexity discussion, and a public code URL. The manuscript is also visually well organized (:codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xa7ae03b/call-61a05524cdbb49b39b0d1219d8854497/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}).
The work uses established public benchmarks and presents no material ethical or misuse concern.
weaknesses: The central theory is incorrect as stated. Theorem 1 silently removes the class priors and class-specific concentrations from the stated vMF posterior, substitutes aggregate quantities for per-node distances, and asserts unsupported bounds. More fundamentally, entropy is not monotone in distance from the true centroid: a point near an incorrect centroid can have large geometric-imbalance score but low entropy. The unnormalized minority scatter can also grow with sample count while average entropy remains bounded, precluding the claimed general proportionality.

Theorem 2 is directly contradicted by its fixed-feature-extractor and fixed-center premise, under which changing the labeled class ratio cannot change the embeddings or geometric score. Withholding labels also does not imply that minority nodes acquire more majority-class neighbors. The proof assumes without justification that a bounded neighborhood fraction is proportional to rho, uses a generally false norm inequality, derives proportionality to rho squared, and then concludes proportionality to rho.

Theorem 3 operates on a weighted sum of rankings without defining how ranked lists are added. Its endpoint calculation provides no guarantee that geometric imbalance is reduced. Moreover, the confidence weight increases only until RBO equals 0.5 and then decreases, contrary to the claimed general training dynamic.

The proposed definition is essentially normalized within-class scatter and requires true labels for unlabeled nodes; it does not specifically measure near-equidistance to competing centroids. The deployed DGIS margin is a different quantity, with no proof that it approximates the definition. Likewise, the vMF/hyperspherical analysis is disconnected from the actual Euclidean K-means method, for which embedding normalization is not specified. DPAM also closely resembles the previously described M3S cluster-consistency filter, limiting methodological originality.

The evaluation does not establish a fair compute or tuning comparison. UNREAL tunes many interacting hyperparameters and performs 40–100 self-training rounds with up to 2000 epochs per round, while several baselines use official settings. The runtime table omits this repeated retraining cost. Final selected configurations, OGB settings, distance definitions, warm-start behavior, and removal of selected nodes from the unlabeled pool are not fully specified.

Several empirical claims overstate the tables: UNREAL has negative deltas on some backbone/dataset combinations despite claims of consistent superiority; the ablation table contains no coherent all-components configuration and DGIS often lowers F1; Computers-Random is reported with conflicting imbalance ratios; and standard errors versus standard deviations are described inconsistently. High-ratio experiments also switch split construction and total label budgets, confounding cross-ratio conclusions. strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem and offers an intuitive embedding-space perspective on why minority-class pseudo-labels can be unreliable.
UNREAL combines classifier–clustering agreement, centroid-based ranking, and ambiguity filtering in a modular, backbone-agnostic self-training framework.

The empirical study is unusually broad: multiple imbalance ratios, natural and synthetic imbalance, three GNN backbones, large and heterophilous graphs, five-run error bars, pseudo-label diagnostics, sensitivity analyses, and runtime measurements. Several Cora and CiteSeer results show substantial gains.
A code link, pseudocode, dataset statistics, hyperparameter ranges, and compute information are provided. The work uses established public benchmarks and presents no material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central theory is incorrect. Theorem 1 relates average entropy to an unnormalized sum over minority nodes, so duplicating nodes changes Dintra without changing average entropy. Its proof silently removes class priors and unequal vMF concentrations, makes unsupported distance assumptions, derives mutually inconsistent lower bounds, and presents a sandwich inequality that does not imply proportionality.

Theorem 2 is directly contradicted by its assumptions: with the feature extractor and class centers fixed, the defined geometric score does not depend on the labeled class-count ratio. The cross-class-neighbor fraction is determined by the graph and true labels, not by how many training labels are retained. The proof also asserts proportionality to rho squared and then concludes proportionality to rho without justification.

The proposed geometric score requires an unlabeled node's ground-truth class and measures distance from that class center rather than ambiguity between competing centers. DGIS instead uses a nearest-versus-second-nearest margin, but no result connects this surrogate to the definition. The claimed Riemannian/vMF analysis is also disconnected from the implemented Euclidean k-means pipeline, and the required hyperspherical distributional assumptions are not validated.

Node-Reordering is not mathematically or algorithmically well specified: ranked lists cannot simply be multiplied and added without defining a rank-vector or score representation. Theorem 3 is a tautology about the chosen weights and proves no reduction in geometric imbalance; moreover, the confidence weight increases only until RBO equals 0.5 and then decreases, contrary to the stated monotonic interpretation.

The headline ablation is internally contradictory. In Tables 1 and 32, the highest F1 row in all four settings has Node-Reordering and DGIS marked off, and its values exactly match the reported full-method results, while the text claims Node-Reordering plus DGIS is best in three settings. This leaves both component attribution and the identity of the evaluated method unresolved.

Empirical claims repeatedly overstate the tables: UNREAL loses on Computers-Random with SAGE, Flickr GAT balanced accuracy, CS-Random SAGE F1, and other settings despite claims of consistent superiority. Duplicate Ogbn-arxiv tables contain different values, natural-imbalance ratios vary across sections, and error bars are inconsistently described as standard errors versus standard deviations. No significance tests support statements of statistical significance.

The comparison protocol may favor UNREAL: it receives a very large per-dataset search over cluster count, rounds, per-class additions, RBO parameters, filtering thresholds, depth, width, and learning rate, whereas GraphSR and BIM use official fixed settings. Selected configurations and split seeds are absent, and the directly relevant 2025 IceBerg method is discussed but not evaluated.

Originality is limited without sharper differentiation from M3S-style clustering/classifier agreement, standard centroid-margin filtering, and conventional class-balanced pseudo-label addition. The per-class addition cap—likely an important rebalancing mechanism—is not isolated. End-to-end efficiency is also unclear because runtime comparisons omit retraining for as many as 100 rounds of up to 2000 epochs. These issues, together with the invalid central theory, require substantially more than a minor revision.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important practical problem and offers an intuitive perspective on why minority-class pseudo-labels can be unreliable. The presentation and figures are generally clear. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-qy3g62rm/call-db71a32eb29347eab39925bd19d87dfb/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
UNREAL is modular and compatible with multiple GNN backbones; consensus filtering, centroid-based ranking, and ambiguity filtering form a practically plausible self-training pipeline.

The evaluation is unusually broad, spanning several imbalance ratios, architectures, naturally imbalanced and large-scale graphs, heterophilous graphs, five-run uncertainty estimates, sensitivity analyses, and pseudo-label diagnostics. Many reported improvements are substantial.
Public benchmarks and a code URL are provided, and the paper reports pseudocode, hyperparameter ranges, and hardware. The research uses standard public data and raises no material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is not established and is generally false. Entropy is not determined by Dintra/Dinter: it also depends on all node-to-center distances, class priors, and concentration parameters. The proof drops priors and class-specific concentrations, substitutes aggregate sums for per-node distances, invokes unjustified bounds, and concludes proportionality from inequalities that do not imply it. A point confidently assigned to the wrong center can have large G but low entropy, directly contradicting the claim.

Theorem 2 is also unsupported. With the feature extractor and centers fixed, changing the labeled-class ratio does not change embeddings or G; withholding labels likewise does not alter cross-class neighborhood proportions. The proof merely assumes E[beta] increases with rho, uses an invalid deviation inequality, derives proportionality to rho squared, and then concludes proportionality to rho. This invalidates the central causal claim about message passing.

The theory and algorithm are poorly connected. The proposed score requires unavailable ground-truth labels, measures distance from the true center rather than ambiguity among centers, and uses Euclidean chordal distances despite the Riemannian framing. Standard experimental models are not shown to satisfy the normalized-vMF assumptions, while DGIS uses a different nearest/second-nearest-center margin for which no guarantee is given.

Node-Reordering is not mathematically or algorithmically well defined: ranked lists are multiplied and added without defining rank vectors, normalization, ordering, or tie handling. Its confidence weight is not monotone over the full RBO range. Theorem 3 only evaluates two limiting cases and proves neither improved ranking quality nor reduced geometric imbalance.

The ablation evidence contradicts the narrative. In every block of Table 32, the highest F1 is in the row where both Node-Reordering and DGIS are marked disabled, while the claimed full configuration is absent. A matched class-balanced self-training control is also needed, and the recent, directly relevant IceBerg method is discussed but not evaluated. Consequently, gains cannot be attributed convincingly to the proposed geometric mechanisms, and novelty beyond established clustering/classifier agreement methods such as M3S remains limited.

Several empirical claims are overstated because UNREAL is not consistently best, and many small differences lack significance testing. The paper alternates between standard errors and standard deviations. Its runtime comparison omits the dominant total cost of 40–100 retraining rounds of up to 2,000 epochs plus repeated clustering, and selected configurations for several added benchmarks are missing. These reproducibility and evaluation issues, together with the invalid headline theory, outweigh the promising empirical results.

weaknesses: The proposed geometric-imbalance score does not actually measure the stated near-equidistance ambiguity: it is the distance to the ground-truth class center divided by global between-center scatter. It requires unavailable labels, is sensitive to the number and arrangement of classes, and can assign identical scores to points having very different decision margins. The operational DGIS margin score is fundamentally different, with no result connecting the two.

Theorem 1 is not validly established. Its proof drops the class priors and class-specific concentrations from the stated vMF model, substitutes dataset-level aggregates for per-node distances, and invokes unsupported bounds. For C=2, the claimed inequality involving epsilon log(C-1) is immediately impossible when the right side is positive. The final sandwich inequality is inconsistent with the preceding derivation and would not imply proportionality anyway.

Theorem 2 contradicts its own assumptions. With a fixed feature extractor and fixed centers, the score cannot change merely because the labeled-set imbalance ratio changes. The neighborhood mixing coefficient depends on the graph's true class composition, not on which labels are observed, and no graph model is given under which it increases with the labeled ratio. The norm inequality used is false in general, and the proof derives proportionality to rho squared before concluding proportionality to rho.

Node-Reordering is mathematically and algorithmically undefined because ordered lists cannot be scalar-multiplied and added as written. Even if list positions are intended, the geometric ranking always receives at least half the weight, and both extreme RBO limits return the geometric ranking. Theorem 3 merely evaluates these limits and proves neither reduced imbalance nor improved selection.

The theory analyzes normalized embeddings with a vMF classifier, whereas the implemented pipeline uses ordinary GNN embeddings, Euclidean K-means, centroids, and an MLP classifier; normalization and the vMF classifier do not appear in the algorithm. The claimed efficiency motivation is also incorrect: the Definition 1 denominator can be precomputed, while DGIS itself requires distances to all class centroids.

The ablation is internally damaging. In Tables 1 and 32, the highlighted best values in all four settings—and the corresponding headline 'Ours' results—come from the row printed with both Node-Reordering and DGIS disabled. The text instead claims that Node-Reordering plus DGIS is best in three of four settings, and no clearly identified full configuration is evaluated. Thus it is unclear which algorithm produces the main results.

The evidence for the geometric claims is weak and confounded: fitted curves are shown only for Cora without raw correlations, uncertainty, or controlled causal tests; entropy and geometry are outputs of the same trained model; and t-SNE plots cannot validate hyperspherical distances. The balanced-pretraining/fine-tuning comparison also does not isolate message passing from architecture and optimization effects.

Claims of consistent superiority are false: the method loses substantially for Computers-Random with GraphSAGE and loses on Flickr-GAT balanced accuracy and CS-GraphSAGE F1. Several large-scale gains are comparable to reported errors, without statistical tests. Dataset counts, imbalance ratios, and uncertainty definitions are inconsistent across sections—for example, Computers-Random is reported with rho approximately 17.7 and 25.5, and errors are variously called standard errors and standard deviations.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link. Exact selected configurations and settings for OGB and heterophilous experiments are absent; split-overlap prevention, seeds, distance definitions, and rank-fusion implementation are unclear. The method tunes many hyperparameters and performs 40–100 rounds of repeated training, but runtime tables report isolated per-training/per-selection costs rather than end-to-end time or total compute.

Originality is insufficiently established. The named geometric phenomenon largely reuses standard within-class scatter, between-class separation, and decision-margin ideas, while the algorithm combines familiar classifier-cluster agreement, centroid ranking, and filtering. Its distinction from M3S, co-training, metric-learning, and prior long-tail representation analyses is not developed adequately, and the manuscript lacks an honest limitations section despite claiming otherwise in the checklist.
